summary: Argues that pervasive monitoring is a technical attack that should be mitigated in the design of IETF protocols where possible. It is a Best Current Practice statement of IETF consensus.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7258 states that pervasive monitoring is an attack on privacy in the technical sense used by the IETF. It commits the IETF to consider ways to make this monitoring harder, more costly, or easier to detect through protocol design.

questions: does the ietf require a pervasive monitoring section
subtitle: The IETF consensus that pervasive monitoring is a technical attack to mitigate where possible.

tldr.problem: Large-scale, often covert monitoring can collect communication content and metadata, affecting the privacy of Internet users and organizations.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF records consensus that pervasive monitoring is an attack in the technical sense and commits to designing protocols that make it more expensive or easier to detect where possible.
tldr.outcome: Protocol authors should be able to explain whether pervasive monitoring is relevant and how they considered it. The document does not prescribe specific technical mechanisms.

today: RFC 7258 is a Best Current Practice published in May 2014. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: What Pervasive Monitoring Means
sections.content:
Pervasive Monitoring (PM) is widespread, often covert surveillance that gathers protocol artifacts, including application content and metadata such as headers. Techniques may include wiretaps, traffic analysis, and obtaining cryptographic keys.

The IETF's technical assessment is that indiscriminate, large-scale monitoring attacks the privacy of Internet users and organizations. In this document, an attack means behavior that subverts communicating parties' intent without their agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: Pervasive monitoring collects communication content or metadata on a broad scale, often without people's knowledge. The IETF treats this as an attack because it reveals information without the communicating parties' agreement.

sections.title: Attack Does Not Describe Motivation
sections.content:
The RFC uses “attack” as a technical term. It refers to actions that change, record, or reveal information about communication without the parties' agreement, regardless of the actor's motive.

The same monitoring techniques can be used for different purposes. The RFC therefore says that motive does not change how protocol designers should consider technical mitigation.
sections.plainLanguage: Here, “attack” describes what happens to communication, not why someone does it. Protocol designers should consider the technique and its effects, regardless of the actor's stated reason.

sections.title: The IETF Commitment to Mitigation
sections.content:
Mitigation does not mean that an attack becomes impossible. A protocol may make monitoring more expensive, make covert monitoring overt, or increase the chance that it will be detected.

The RFC notes that existing security standards generally do not address pervasive monitoring, metadata confidentiality, traffic analysis, or data minimization. Protocol authors should be able to explain whether PM applies to their work and how they considered it; a separate PM section is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: Mitigation can make monitoring harder or easier to detect, even if it cannot prevent it completely. Protocol authors need a reasoned answer about whether monitoring matters to their design.

sections.title: Balancing Monitoring and Its Uses
sections.content:
Some monitoring supports network management or anti-spam systems. The RFC also gives certificate transparency as an example of monitoring that can help detect some monitoring attacks.

Monitoring tools may still be abused for pervasive monitoring. Protocol designers need to weigh that risk while recognizing that making networks unmanageable is not an acceptable mitigation.
sections.plainLanguage: Some monitoring supports useful network functions, but the same mechanisms can be misused. Protocol design should consider both the privacy risk and the need to operate networks.

sections.title: Limits of the IETF's Role
sections.content:
The IETF develops standards but does not control how they are implemented or deployed. It also does not standardize every layer of the protocol stack.

Legal and political responses to pervasive monitoring are outside the IETF's technical scope. The RFC says the broader Internet community must also act if pervasive monitoring is to be fully addressed.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF can change protocol specifications but cannot control their deployment or address legal and political issues. Other parts of the Internet community also have a role.

sections.title: How the Consensus Was Published
sections.content:
Earlier architectural statements, including RFC 1984 and RFC 2804, were published jointly by the IESG and the Internet Architecture Board. The IETF and IAB later separated their publication streams.

RFC 7258 followed discussions in both groups but was published as an IETF-stream consensus document to represent the IETF community as a whole.
sections.plainLanguage: This document records the IETF community's consensus. It was published in the IETF stream after the IETF and IAB had separated their publication processes.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content: The RFC is about privacy and points to RFC 6973 for discussion of the relationship between privacy and security threats. That document treats surveillance as a combined security and privacy threat.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC concerns privacy. It directs readers to RFC 6973 for a broader discussion of surveillance as both a security and privacy threat.
